title: Rise of Rome (Republic to Empire)
summary: Between the traditional founding of the Republic in 509 BCE and Augustus's settlement of 27 BCE, the city-state of Rome conquered Italy, destroyed Carthage, absorbed Greece and much of western Asia, and turned through civil war into a monarchy ruling the Mediterranean.
card: Rome grew from Iron Age huts by the Tiber into a city ruled first by kings and then, by the traditional reckoning from 509 BCE, by an aristocratic republic. Over the next five centuries it subdued Italy, won three wars against Carthage and took over the Greek east, enslaving hundreds of thousands of people as it went. The strains of that empire wrecked the Republic in a century of political killings and civil wars, from which Caesar's heir Octavian emerged as sole ruler, renamed Augustus in 27 BCE.
what:
Roman tradition said that Romulus founded the city on the Palatine Hill in 753 BCE; UNESCO and modern scholars present that date as legend. Archaeology shows a hut settlement instead: the Metropolitan Museum dates the first cluster of huts to the 10th century BCE, while the post-holes cut into the Palatine bedrock are dated by Diana Kleiner of Yale to the 8th century BCE. Kings ruled the early city, the later ones Etruscan; from 509 BCE, by the conventional chronology, a republic of elected magistrates replaced them. A long contest between the patrician aristocracy and the plebeians ended in 287 BCE with a mixed patrician-plebeian nobility.

Polybius describes expansion in stages. After recovering from a Gallic capture of the city, the Romans subdued the Latins, Etruscans, Samnites and Italian Celts and drove out Pyrrhus, making most of Italy subject to them. In 264 BCE they crossed to Sicily, opening three Punic Wars against Carthage (264–241, 218–201 and 149–146 BCE). Hannibal invaded Italy across the Alps and crushed a Roman army at Cannae in 216 BCE, but Scipio Africanus defeated him at Zama in 202 BCE. Polybius, writing in Greek, marvelled that Rome brought nearly the whole known world under its rule in under 53 years from the Hannibalic war. In 167 BCE, after the defeat of Macedon, Roman troops sacked Epirus and, by the ancient count, sold 150,000 people into slavery; in 146 BCE Carthage was razed and its land became the province of Africa.

Conquest brought wealth, captives and widening inequality. The killing of the tribune Tiberius Gracchus in 133 BCE began a century of political violence: the Social War with Rome's Italian allies from 91 BCE, the slave revolt led by Spartacus from 73 BCE and the wars of the great generals. Julius Caesar conquered Gaul, accepted the dictatorship for life and was stabbed to death at a senate meeting on 15 March 44 BCE. His heir Octavian defeated his rivals, finally at Actium in 31 BCE, and in January 27 BCE the senate named him Augustus. Sources disagree over the founding (legend versus excavation) and over how far Augustus restored or replaced the Republic.

uncertainty.note: 509 BCE is the conventional (Varronian) date for the end of the monarchy, inherited from Roman annalistic chronology and not independently fixed; early Republican dates may be off by several years. The end date is secure: the senate's grant of the name Augustus, dated by the Loeb editor of the Res Gestae to 16 January 27 BCE (Julian calendar). The traditional founding of the city (753 BCE) is legendary and is not used as the record's start.

how: Polybius explains the first phase as a sequence of wars fought outward from Latium: once Rome had subdued the Latins, Etruscans, Samnites and Italian Celts and expelled Pyrrhus, it controlled the manpower of most of Italy, and the war over Sicily from 264 BCE drew it into a contest with Carthage at sea. Victory over Hannibal, in Polybius's reading, convinced the Romans that they could reach for Greece and Asia, and the defeat of Macedon in 168 BCE was followed by exemplary terror in Epirus in 167 BCE. Conquered land outside Italy was organised as provinces paying tribute; Caesar alone imposed 40 million sesterces a year on Gaul, according to Suetonius. Wars also fed a vast trade in captives: Scheidel models an inflow of 2 to 4 million slaves into Italy over the last two centuries BCE. Wealth flowed unevenly, and the Met attributes the Republic's collapse to the strain of permanent military commitment and the gulf between those who profited and those impoverished. The Gracchi tried to redistribute public land through a three-man commission and were killed in 133 and 121 BCE. The Social War of 91–88 BCE forced Rome to extend citizenship to its Italian allies. Commanders whose soldiers looked to them for reward then fought one another; Caesar's dictatorship ended in his assassination, and Octavian, who had raised a private army at nineteen, finished the civil wars and in 28–27 BCE recast his power as a restored republic under his leadership.
why_it_matters: This process created the state that, in UNESCO's words, dominated the Mediterranean world for many centuries, with Rome as its capital. By 27 BCE a single city governed provinces from Spain to Syria and from Gaul to Africa, and its Augustan census counted 4,063,000 citizens in 28 BCE. UNESCO credits the city with spreading law, language and literature that became the basis of Western culture. The same expansion ended other worlds: Carthage, the capital of Punic civilization in Africa, was razed in 146 BCE, and wars of conquest moved an estimated 2 to 4 million captives into slavery in Italy in the last two centuries BCE alone. The Republic's failure also produced a new political form: Augustus presented his monarchy as a restored republic in which he merely outranked his colleagues, while the Met describes his position as complete control. A counterfactual shows how contingent this was: had Hannibal's victories after Cannae in 216 BCE broken Rome's hold on Italy, the western Mediterranean would probably have remained divided between Punic and Roman spheres, and the rapid absorption of the Greek east that Polybius dated from the Hannibalic war could not have followed. Without the political violence that began with Tiberius Gracchus, the Republic might have absorbed its empire through institutions rather than through warlords, and the Principate need not have emerged in the form Augustus gave it.

related.because: The territorial empire assembled between 509 and 27 BCE, and the one-man rule Augustus built over it, became the state whose western provinces fragmented between 376 and 476 CE.

perspectives.holder: Roman tradition, as reported by UNESCO and in Kleiner's Yale lecture
perspectives.account: Romulus (with Remus, in the UNESCO wording) founded Rome on the Palatine in 753 BCE, traditionally on 21 April. This is recorded as a belief about origins, labelled legendary.

perspectives.holder: Archaeological evidence, summarised by the Metropolitan Museum and by Diana Kleiner
perspectives.account: Rome began as a cluster of Iron Age huts; the Met dates the first huts to the 10th century BCE, and Kleiner describes post-hole huts cut into the Palatine tufa in the 8th century BCE, with hut-shaped cremation urns as supporting evidence.
After ending the civil wars he handed the state back to the senate and people in 28–27 BCE, and thereafter outranked others in prestige but held no more formal power than his colleagues in office.

perspectives.holder: Metropolitan Museum of Art (modern historical summary)
perspectives.account: Octavian removed all opposition to his complete control of the Roman state before receiving the title Augustus in 27 BCE; the Republic had collapsed under the strains of empire.

perspectives.holder: Polybius, as reported by Antoniadis and Pliakou (2022); Plutarch, Aemilius Paulus 29
perspectives.account: In 167 BCE, on the senate's order, Aemilius Paullus's army destroyed 70 Epirote cities in one day and sold 150,000 people, mostly Molossians, into slavery.

perspectives.holder: Antoniadis and Pliakou (2022), from surveys and excavations of the last 30 years
perspectives.account: Many, though not all, Epirote settlements survived the 167 BCE destructions, so the ancient picture of total devastation needs qualifying; the enslavement figure itself cannot be checked archaeologically.

importance.justification: Rome's growth from city-state to Mediterranean empire shaped the political, legal, linguistic and religious history of Europe, North Africa and western Asia for centuries, so it must be visible at whole-planet view.
